quests.instruction: Read it in one smooth flow, linking the words (linking: consonant + vowel).
quests.hint: Listen for the links: 'turn it off' sounds like 'tur-ni-toff', and 'take it out of' sounds like 'ta-ki-tou-tuv'.
quests.explanation: When a word ends in a consonant and the next begins with a vowel, the consonant slides across to start the next syllable. Say the phrase as a chain, not as separate words.
quests.textToSpeak: Turn it off, then take it out of the box.
quests.phoneticHint: 'turn it off' is [ˈtɜːr.nɪ.ˈtɔːf] and 'take it out of' is [ˈteɪ.kɪ.ˈtaʊ.təv].
commonMistakes: Pausing between the words: 'turn – it – off'
Adding a glottal stop before each vowel
Giving every word its full stress

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would talk to a friend.
quests.hint: 'ran out of' and 'pick up a' each link into one flowing chunk: ra-nou-tuv, pi-ku-pə.
quests.explanation: Each final consonant slides onto the next vowel: n into 'out', t into 'of', k into 'up', p into 'a'. The chunk feels like a single word of three or four syllables.
quests.textToSpeak: I ran out of coffee, so I'll pick up a bag after work.
quests.phoneticHint: 'ran out of' is [ˈræ.naʊ.təv] and 'pick up a' is [ˈpɪ.kʌ.pə].
commonMistakes: Dropping the [t] in 'out' instead of linking it

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a polite request at a hotel.
quests.hint: Link 'ask if it's OK' and 'leave a bag': 'a-skif-its-oh-KAY', 'lee-va-bag'.
quests.explanation: This request is full of consonant-to-vowel links: ask+if, it's+OK, leave+a, here+until. The result sounds smoother and more polite.
quests.textToSpeak: Could I ask if it's OK to leave a bag here until eight?
quests.phoneticHint: 'ask if it's OK' is [ə.ˈskɪ.fɪts oʊ.ˈkeɪ] and 'leave a' is [ˈliː.və].
commonMistakes: Saying 'leave a' as two separate words with a gap

quests.instruction: Read it in one smooth flow, linking the words (same-consonant linking).
quests.hint: 'black coffee' and 'big game' each have the same consonant at the boundary: [k]+[k] and [g]+[g]. Say each as one long sound.
quests.explanation: When two identical consonants meet, hold the closure once and release once. You don't say two separate sounds; the only trace is a slightly longer pause.
quests.textToSpeak: Let's get a black coffee before the big game.
quests.phoneticHint: 'black coffee' is [blæk ˈkɒfi] with a single held [k]; 'big game' is [bɪg ˈgeɪm] with a single held [g].
commonMistakes: Saying two separate [k] sounds with a release
Dropping the first consonant so 'black' sounds like 'bla'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a positive reaction.
quests.hint: 'good deal' joins [d]+[d], and 'some more' joins [m]+[m].
quests.explanation: Hold the tongue on the ridge for one long [d]; keep the lips closed for one long [m]. The second word begins as you release.
quests.textToSpeak: That's a good deal; I'll take some more of them.
quests.phoneticHint: 'good deal' is [gʊd ˈdiːl] with one long [d]; 'some more' is [səm ˈmɔːr] with one long [m].
commonMistakes: Adding a vowel between the two words

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would arrange to meet.
quests.hint: 'next Tuesday' joins [t]+[t]; 'this side' joins [s]+[s].
quests.explanation: For [s]+[s], keep the hiss going a little longer. For [t]+[t], hold the tongue on the ridge once. Don't insert a break.
quests.textToSpeak: Let's meet next Tuesday, on this side of the street.
quests.phoneticHint: 'next Tuesday' is [nekst ˈtuːzdeɪ], with a single held [t]; 'this side' is [ðɪs ˈsaɪd], with one long [s].

quests.instruction: Read it in one smooth flow, linking the words ([w] glide between vowels).
quests.hint: After [aʊ] and [uː], a small [w] glide fills the gap: how-w-are, do-w-it, who-w-is.
quests.explanation: Round the lips a little as you move from one vowel to the next; you're making a very short [w] without any break.
quests.textToSpeak: How are you going to do it, and who is coming?
quests.phoneticHint: 'how are' is [haʊ.wɑːr], 'do it' is [duː.wɪt], and 'who is' is [huː.wɪz].
commonMistakes: Stopping the voice between the vowels
Saying 'do it' as 'doo-eet' with a full [iː]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a firm agreement.
quests.hint: After [iː] and [aɪ], a small [j] glide links the words: the-y-answer, she-y-agreed, I-y-approved.
quests.explanation: Spread the lips slightly and glide the tongue toward the palate. It's a quick [j] between the two vowels.
quests.textToSpeak: The answer is obvious; she agreed, and I approved it too.
quests.phoneticHint: 'the answer' is [ðiː.jæn.sər], 'she agreed' is [ʃiː.jə.griːd], and 'I approved' is [aɪ.jə.pruːvd].
commonMistakes: Adding a glottal stop before the second word

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a social invitation.
quests.hint: 'go out' and 'know a' both pick up a [w]: go-w-out, know-w-a.
quests.explanation: [oʊ] ends with rounded lips, so the [w] happens naturally before the next vowel. Don't close the throat between the words.
quests.textToSpeak: Let's go out tonight; I know a place that's open late.
quests.phoneticHint: 'go out' is [goʊ.waʊt] and 'know a' is [noʊ.wə].
commonMistakes: Saying 'know a' as 'no-ah' with separate vowels

quests.instruction: Read it in one smooth flow, linking the words (linking [r]).
quests.hint: The [r] in 'far', 'there' and 'hour' is pronounced when a vowel follows: far-r-away, there-r-in, hour-r-or.
quests.explanation: In accents that drop [r] before a consonant, the [r] returns before a vowel. In rhotic accents, it is always pronounced and simply links.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm not far away; I'll be there in an hour or so.
quests.phoneticHint: 'far away' is [fɑː.rə.ˈweɪ], 'there in' is [ðeə.rɪn], and 'hour or' is [aʊə.rɔː].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would describe a booking.
quests.hint: Listen for [r] linking into a vowel: after-r-eight, there-r-are, four-r-of, or-r-maybe.
quests.explanation: The [r] belongs to the first word but is pronounced as the start of the next syllable. Keep it soft and short.
quests.textToSpeak: After eight there are four of us, or maybe more.
quests.phoneticHint: 'after eight' is [ˈæf.tə.reɪt], 'there are' is [ðeə.rɑːr], and 'four of' is [fɔː.rəv].
commonMistakes: Putting a gap between 'four' and 'of', so the [r] disappears
Making the [r] too strong or rolled

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a casual remark.
quests.hint: In some accents, a small [r] appears between 'idea' and 'about', and between 'saw' and 'it', even though there is no r in the spelling.
quests.explanation: In non-rhotic accents, speakers add [r] between two vowels to avoid a gap. It is optional; if you speak American English, you can link the vowels with a glide instead.
quests.textToSpeak: I've no idea about it, and I saw it on the news yesterday.
quests.phoneticHint: 'idea about' is [aɪ.ˈdɪə.rə.ˈbaʊt] and 'saw it' is [sɔː.rɪt] in accents that use intrusive [r].
commonMistakes: Leaving a pause between the vowels
Adding an [r] where a consonant follows the vowel
Stopping the voice with a glottal stop

quests.instruction: Read it in one smooth flow, linking the words (dropped [t] in clusters).
quests.hint: The [t] in 'last part' and 'next week' is barely heard: las-part, nex-week.
quests.explanation: When a word ends in [st] or [kst] and the next word starts with a consonant, the [t] is usually not released. The tongue may touch, but no burst is heard.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll finish the last part next week.
quests.phoneticHint: 'last part' is [læs pɑːrt] and 'next week' is [neks wiːk].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a supportive comment.
quests.hint: 'best friend' and 'hard time' lose or soften the last stop: bes-friend, har-time.
quests.explanation: In fast speech, [t] and [d] at the end of the first word are held or dropped before another consonant. The meaning stays clear.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll ask my best friend; she's had a hard time too.
quests.phoneticHint: 'best friend' is [bes frend] and 'hard time' is [hɑːr taɪm].
commonMistakes: Pronouncing 'best' and 'hard' as fully separate words
Making the [d] of 'hard' into a full syllable

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a reminder.
quests.hint: 'don't want', 'first meeting' and 'next Monday' each contain a [t] that is often dropped: don-wan, firs-meeting, nex-Monday.
quests.explanation: Speakers drop [t] between two other consonants. Do it only in fast, casual speech; keep it in careful speech.
quests.textToSpeak: We don't want to miss the first meeting next Monday.
quests.phoneticHint: 'don't want' is [doʊn wɒn], 'first meeting' is [fɜːrs ˈmiːtɪŋ], and 'next Monday' is [neks ˈmʌndeɪ].

quests.instruction: Read it in one smooth flow, linking the words (assimilation: [n]→[m], [t]→[p]).
quests.hint: 'ten people' sounds like 'tem people', and 'that boy' sounds like 'thap boy'.
quests.explanation: The final sound moves to match the place of the next one: [n] becomes [m] before [p], and [t] becomes [p] before [b].
quests.textToSpeak: Ten people applied, but that boy got the job.
quests.phoneticHint: 'ten people' is [tem ˈpiːpəl] and 'that boy' is [ðæp ˈbɔɪ].
commonMistakes: Keeping the tongue on the ridge for [n]
Saying 'ten' and 'people' as two separate beats with a clear tongue tap

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a travel note.
quests.hint: 'in Berlin' sounds like 'im Berlin', and 'in case' sounds like 'ing case'.
quests.explanation: [n] takes the place of the next consonant: before [b] it becomes [m]; before [k] it becomes [ŋ]. The mouth prepares early.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll be in Berlin in June, in case you want to meet.
quests.phoneticHint: 'in Berlin' is [ɪm bɜːrˈlɪn] and 'in case' is [ɪŋ ˈkeɪs].
commonMistakes: Keeping a clear [n] with tongue contact

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a sick-day note.
quests.hint: 'bad cold' sounds like 'bag cold', and 'hot cup' sounds like 'hock cup'.
quests.explanation: [d] becomes [g] and [t] becomes [k] before a [k] sound. The tongue goes straight to the back position.
quests.textToSpeak: I've got a bad cold, so I'm staying in bed with a hot cup of tea.
quests.phoneticHint: 'bad cold' is [bæg koʊld] and 'hot cup' is [hɒk kʌp].
commonMistakes: Stopping the voice after 'bad', so it is separated from 'cold'

quests.instruction: Read it in one smooth flow, linking the words ([t]+[j]→[tʃ], [d]+[j]→[dʒ]).
quests.hint: 'don't you' sounds like 'don-chu', and 'did you' sounds like 'did-ju'.
quests.explanation: When [t] or [d] meets 'you', the sounds fuse into [tʃ] or [dʒ]. Your tongue doesn't separate; it slides straight into the new sound.
quests.textToSpeak: Don't you think it's too late? Did you tell them?
quests.phoneticHint: 'don't you' is [ˈdoʊn.tʃu] and 'did you' is [ˈdɪ.dʒu].
commonMistakes: Separating the words with a clear [t]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would in a first meeting.
quests.hint: 'meet you' sounds like 'mee-chu' and 'did you' sounds like 'did-ju'.
quests.explanation: In a friendly first meeting, the fusion sounds natural. [t]+[j] gives [tʃ]; [d]+[j] gives [dʒ].
quests.textToSpeak: Nice to meet you. Where did you grow up?
quests.phoneticHint: 'meet you' is [ˈmiː.tʃu] and 'did you' is [ˈdɪ.dʒu].
commonMistakes: Pronouncing 'meet' and 'you' as two separate words

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a polite explanation.
quests.hint: 'as you' sounds like 'a-zhu', and 'unless you' sounds like 'un-less-shu'.
quests.explanation: [z]+[j] fuses into [ʒ], and [s]+[j] fuses into [ʃ]. The fricative slides directly into the new sound.
quests.textToSpeak: As you know, I can't stay long, unless you need me to.
quests.phoneticHint: 'as you' is [əˈʒju] and 'unless you' is [ənˈleʃ.ʃu].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would before a trip.
quests.hint: In American English, the [t] in 'better' and 'water' is a quick tap, close to [d].
quests.explanation: Between vowels, when the first is stressed, [t] becomes a light tap of the tongue on the ridge. British speakers often keep [t]; both are fine.
quests.textToSpeak: I'd better get some water before we go.
quests.phoneticHint: 'better' is [ˈbeɾər] and 'water' is [ˈwɔːɾər].
commonMistakes: Making a heavy [t] burst in each word
Turning it into a long, full [d]

quests.instruction: Say it at conversation speed and let the small words shrink (flap [ɾ] across word boundaries).
quests.hint: The [t] joins the next vowel in 'wait a' and 'put it in' and becomes a tap.
quests.explanation: At the end of a word, before a vowel, [t] becomes a tap: 'wait a' sounds like 'wai-da', and 'put it in' like 'pu-di-din'.
quests.textToSpeak: Wait a minute; I forgot to put it in the suitcase.
quests.phoneticHint: 'wait a' is [ˈweɪ.ɾə] and 'put it in' is [ˈpʊ.ɾɪ.ɾɪn].
commonMistakes: Saying a clear [t] with a burst

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a story about an event.
quests.hint: 'a lot of', 'got up', 'a little bit of' and 'matter' all contain a tap.
quests.explanation: Any [t] between two vowels, including across word boundaries, can be a tap in American English. The phrases run together like one word.
quests.textToSpeak: A lot of people got up early, but a little bit of rain didn't matter.
quests.phoneticHint: 'a lot of' is [ə.ˈlɑː.ɾə.və], 'got up' is [ˈgɑː.ɾʌp], and 'matter' is [ˈmæ.ɾər].
commonMistakes: Making 'got up' sound like 'got-up' with a hard [t]
Saying 'lot of' as 'lot-of' with a pause

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would explain an errand.
quests.hint: The small words 'to', 'for', 'some', 'and', 'a' and 'of' are weak: tə, fər, səm, ən, ə, əv.
quests.explanation: Function words are unstressed, so their vowels reduce to schwa. The content words 'shop', 'eggs', 'bit' and 'cheese' carry the beat.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm going to the shop for some eggs and a bit of cheese.
quests.targetPhoneme: weak forms: to, for, some, and, of
quests.phoneticHint: [aɪm ˈgoʊɪŋ tə ðə ˈʃɒp fər səm ˈegz ən ə ˈbɪt əv ˈtʃiːz]: only the content words are strong.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a timetable announcement.
quests.hint: 'to', 'the', 'at' and 'and' are weak: tə, ðə, ət, ən.
quests.explanation: 'at' and 'to' are almost swallowed: only 'bus', 'airport', 'leaves', 'nine', 'arrives' and 'ten' are strong.
quests.textToSpeak: The bus to the airport leaves at nine and arrives at ten.
quests.targetPhoneme: weak forms: to, the, at, and
quests.phoneticHint: [ðə ˈbʌs tə ði ˈeərpɔːrt ˈliːvz ət ˈnaɪn ən əˈraɪvz ət ˈten].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would describe a friend.
quests.hint: 'of', 'to' and 'a' are weak; 'been' is weak too: bɪn.
quests.explanation: 'been' is usually [bɪn] in ordinary speech. The phrase 'a lot of' can run together as [ə ˈlɒtəv].
quests.textToSpeak: She's a friend of mine, and we've been to a lot of places together.
quests.targetPhoneme: weak forms: of, been, to, a
quests.phoneticHint: [ʃiz ə ˈfrend əv ˈmaɪn ən wiv bɪn tu ə ˈlɒt əv ˈpleɪsɪz təˈgeðər].
commonMistakes: Giving 'of' a full vowel and a clear [f]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud and make 'can' and 'can't' clearly different.
quests.hint: 'can' is weak [kən], but 'can't' is strong [kænt]. The vowel and the final [t] tell them apart.
quests.explanation: Positive 'can' is reduced and unstressed; negative 'can't' keeps its full vowel and stress. Listeners rely on the vowel difference.
quests.textToSpeak: I can do it on Friday, but I can't do it today.
quests.phoneticHint: [aɪ kən ˈduː ɪt] versus [aɪ ˈkænt ˈduː ɪt]: 'can' is a short schwa syllable and 'can't' is a stressed one.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a worried remark Watch the weak forms: have, was, were, for.
quests.hint: 'have', 'was', 'were' and 'for' are weak: əv, wəz, wər, fər.
quests.explanation: Auxiliary verbs and 'for' reduce in ordinary speech. The content words 'been', 'worried' and 'waiting' carry the stress.
quests.textToSpeak: Where have you been? I was worried; we were waiting for you.
quests.targetPhoneme: weak forms: have, was, were, for
quests.phoneticHint: [ˈweər əv ju ˈbɪn], [aɪ wəz ˈwʌrid], [wi wər ˈweɪtɪŋ fər ju].
commonMistakes: Giving 'have' a full vowel and an [h], as in [hæv]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a relaxed explanation.
quests.hint: 'would have' becomes 'would-uv', 'her' loses its [h], and 'was' is weak: wəd-əv, ər, wəz.
quests.explanation: 'would have' is usually said 'would-uv'. 'her' is [ər] when unstressed. Both signal natural, relaxed speech.
quests.textToSpeak: I would have called her, but I thought she was asleep.
quests.targetPhoneme: weak forms: would have, her, was
quests.phoneticHint: [aɪ wʊd əv ˈkɔːld ər], with 'have' as [əv] and 'her' as [ər].
commonMistakes: Turning 'would have' into a stressed 'would HAVE'
Saying 'was' with a full vowel, as 'woz'
